item.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
choices: Children can learn a neighbor's rules best by being shouted at often.
A person's actions can have reasons that others cannot see at first.
A short way home can be worth more than a neighbor's good opinion.
Small animals can protect their young by blending into the ground.
item.passage:
Every afternoon, Mr. Halvorsen patrolled his front lawn with his arms folded. If any of us cut across the corner of his yard on the way home from school, he waved his cap and shouted, "Around! Go around!"

"He just likes yelling," my friend Kenji said, and I agreed. Walking around his yard added a whole minute to our trip, and Mr. Halvorsen's frown made him look like a storm cloud in a cardigan.

Then one Thursday I dropped my math folder, and the papers scattered across his grass. I froze. Mr. Halvorsen walked over, slowly, and picked up every sheet himself. When he handed them back, he pointed at a patch of gravel near the corner.

"Look," he whispered, "but stay still."

At first I saw only pebbles. Then one of the pebbles blinked. A small brown bird with two black stripes across her chest was sitting right on the ground, on four speckled eggs that looked just like the stones around them.

"Killdeer," he said. "She built her nest right where people walk. I've been guarding it for three weeks."

The next day I told Kenji everything, and we walked the long way around. Mr. Halvorsen was out on the lawn again, arms folded, watching the corner. This time, when he saw us, he lifted his cap instead of waving it.
item.explanation: The children think "He just likes yelling," until they learn "She built her nest right where people walk," so the story shows that "A person's actions can have reasons that others cannot see at first."
item.correct_answer: A person's actions can have reasons that others cannot see at first.

distractor_rationales.reason: The eggs "looked just like the stones around them," but that one detail explains the bird, while the story is about how the narrator comes to understand Mr. Halvorsen.

distractor_rationales.choice: Children can learn a neighbor's rules best by being shouted at often.
distractor_rationales.reason: The children kept cutting across while he "waved his cap and shouted"; they walk "the long way around" only after he shows them the nest, so the shouting is what failed to teach them.

distractor_rationales.choice: A short way home can be worth more than a neighbor's good opinion.
distractor_rationales.reason: Valuing the shortcut is how the children acted at the start, when walking around "added a whole minute to our trip"; by the end they choose "the long way around," so the story does not side with the shortcut.

item.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the poem?
choices: Small things left in pockets can show where a person has been.
A younger child can feel lost inside an older child's things.
A coat that is too large can be useless until it fits.
An object handed down can become the new owner's own.
item.passage:
Coat, you came folded on my bed
the way my brother left you,
sleeves crossed over your chest
like someone waiting to be picked.

Your pockets still hold his weather:
a movie stub gone soft as cloth,
a pebble from a beach I never saw,
one green button from some other coat.

You are too big for me. Your shoulders
slope past mine like a roof past its walls,
your cuffs swallow my hands,
and your hem knocks against my knees
when I run for the corner.

But today the wind came hard off the hill
and you closed around me, all of you,
the way a hand closes around a key
it means to keep.

So I am writing my name
inside your collar, under his,
in ink a little darker.
Next winter, coat, you will fit.
item.explanation: The coat arrives "the way my brother left you," and by the end the speaker is writing a name "inside your collar, under his," which shows that "An object handed down can become the new owner's own."
item.correct_answer: An object handed down can become the new owner's own.

distractor_rationales.choice: A coat that is too large can be useless until it fits.
distractor_rationales.reason: The coat is still too big in stanza 4, yet it already does its job: "you closed around me, all of you" when the wind "came hard off the hill."

distractor_rationales.choice: Small things left in pockets can show where a person has been.
distractor_rationales.reason: The stub, pebble and button in stanza 2 do show "his weather," but that is one stanza; the poem moves on to the speaker claiming the coat.

distractor_rationales.choice: A younger child can feel lost inside an older child's things.
distractor_rationales.reason: Stanza 3 says "You are too big for me," but the poem goes past that feeling to the speaker writing a name in the collar and saying "you will fit."

item.passage:
The walkie-talkie was at the bottom of my closet, its antenna still bent from the time I dropped it off the fire escape. The yellow paint had worn down to gray where my thumb used to press the button.

Two summers ago, Lin and I talked on these every night. Her bedroom window faced mine across the alley, and at nine o'clock exactly one of us would click twice, which meant the channel was open. We reported on everything: our math teacher's new haircut, the cat on the third floor that kept escaping, the ending of a movie we had both promised not to watch yet.

Then, last fall, Lin joined the robotics team. Practice ran late, and she came home tired and full of words I had to ask her to explain, like servos and torque. Some nights her lamp stayed dark at nine. Other nights it was on, and I waited with my thumb on the button, and the click never came. By winter I had stopped waiting. I put the walkie-talkie in the closet and told myself it was a toy anyway.

Now it was June, and across the alley her lamp was on.

I found two batteries in the kitchen drawer. The walkie-talkie hissed when I switched it on, a long sigh of static, and I felt silly holding it up like a little kid. I clicked twice anyway.

Nothing. Then a crackle, and a voice I knew, a little lower than I remembered. "Rosa? Is that you?"

"Channel's open," I said.

She laughed, and then she started talking fast, the way she used to. The team had made it to the regional finals and lost in the last round when a wheel fell off. She had kept her walkie-talkie on her desk the whole year, just in case.

"You could have clicked," I said.

"So could you."

Across the alley, her shadow came to the window and waved. I waved back. Then she started explaining torque again, and this time I asked questions.

Before sunrise she dipped a rag of plain wool into the bucket, then into the last of the madder bath, and hung it on the line to dry.

So Sefa's mother gave her a clay pot with a lid and sent her over the ridge to Aunt Halima's village, where the houses sat higher and stayed dry. Aunt Halima filled the pot with glowing coals. "Feed them a pinch of dry grass now and then," she said, "and they will last you all the way home."

On the rocky island of Teral, a finger-length lizard called the dusk gecko hunts small flies along the sea cliffs at night. People who spot one by flashlight describe it as nearly white. People who find the same gecko the next morning, resting on a sunny ledge, describe it as the color of wet slate.

Biologist Mira Ankeny wanted to know why the gecko changes. Two explanations seemed possible. The first was camouflage: a pale gecko is hard to see on moonlit rock, and a dark one blends into shadowy morning stone. The second was heat. A dark skin soaks up sunlight faster than a pale one, and a cold gecko is too sluggish to catch anything.

Watching geckos on the cliffs could never settle the question. The rock holds the day's warmth long after dark, so on Teral the coldest hour comes just as the sun rises. Light and chill arrive together, so a gecko that darkened at dawn might have been reacting to either one. Ankeny decided to move the problem indoors.

Her team collected thirty geckos and placed them, a few at a time, in four kinds of glass boxes. One box was bright and warm, one bright and cool, one dim and warm, and one dim and cool. Every half hour, a student held a color card beside each gecko and recorded its shade.

The results were clear. Geckos in both cool boxes turned dark within forty minutes, whether their box was bright or dim. Geckos in the warm boxes stayed pale, even under the brightest lamp. Light made almost no difference at all.

Ankeny points out that camouflage may still help the gecko in the wild, since a pale lizard on pale rock is a lucky lizard. But the boxes showed that the gecko's skin takes its cue from temperature. When the morning air is cold, the gecko darkens, and its dark back gathers the first sunlight and warms the animal enough to move quickly again.

When the town of Callow Bay put up its first wind turbine above the harbor, the engineers expected it to run hardest on blustery afternoons. Instead, on quiet spring evenings, when the flags in town hung limp, it kept braking its blades to a stop and sending an alarm to the control office.

The turbine's computer was built to do exactly that if it sensed dangerous shaking. Engineer Dana Whitlock's first guess was that the shaking sensor itself was faulty, reporting tremors that were not there. Her team replaced it. The next calm evening, the turbine stopped again.

Next, Whitlock went through three months of records. The shutdowns were far from random. Almost every one happened within two hours after sunset, and almost every one came on a clear night. Cloudy evenings and breezy evenings rarely caused trouble. Something about calm, clear dusk was shaking the machine.

To find out what, the team borrowed a laser instrument that measures wind speed at different heights by bouncing light off dust in the air. They aimed it straight up beside the turbine on a clear evening. Near the ground, the air barely moved. At 100 meters, the height of the highest blade tip, wind was racing at nearly 40 kilometers per hour.

During the day, sunlight warms the ground, and the warm air churns and mixes, so wind speed is fairly even from bottom to top. After sunset on a clear night, the ground cools quickly, and the lowest layer of air settles and goes still, like syrup at the bottom of a glass. The upper air slides over it without slowing. Each blade, sweeping from the still air at the bottom of its circle to the fast air at the top, was being shoved hard and then released every few seconds.

"We had been judging the wind by what we felt standing next to the tower," Whitlock said. "The turbine was feeling a completely different sky."

The fix turned out to be modest. The team reprogrammed the blades to tilt slightly as they pass through the fast upper layer, which evens out the push. Since then, the turbine has run through every clear spring evening, and Callow Bay now measures wind at several heights before siting its second machine.

A hot-air balloon has a wicker basket, a burner, and a huge fabric bag called the envelope. What it lacks is a steering wheel. So how does a pilot travel from a launch field to a landing spot miles away? The trick is to choose which wind to ride.

Air near the ground often moves differently from air higher up. On a calm morning, the breeze at treetop height might drift east while a layer a few hundred feet above it slides north. Before a flight, pilots release a small helium balloon and watch it rise. If it wanders one way and then bends another, they know the sky is stacked in layers.

Once aloft, the pilot moves between those layers by controlling heat. Pulling the burner's lever sends a roaring flame up into the envelope. The heated air makes the balloon lighter, so it climbs. To descend, the pilot waits for the air inside to cool, or opens a vent at the top to let some hot air escape.

"You can't point a balloon at a field," says Mara Delacroix, who has flown for nineteen years over the farmland around Kessel Ridge. "You find the wind that's already going there and climb into it."

Even a skilled pilot rarely lands exactly where she planned. That is why every flight has a chase crew. Two or three people follow in a truck with a trailer, keeping the balloon in sight and talking with the pilot by radio. When the balloon touches down, the crew helps squeeze the air out of the envelope and roll it up, which can take twenty minutes. Then everyone rides home together in the truck.

item.passage:
When Osei Brandt arrived in Halvern in 1958 to teach high-school chemistry, the town's main streets were wide, dusty, and almost bare. In July the pavement grew so hot that shopkeepers hosed down their sidewalks at noon. Brandt, who had grown up beneath the oaks of a much older city, found the glare hard to bear.

He began with a single maple outside his rented house. The next spring he planted six more along the block, paying for the saplings out of his own salary and watering them from a tank he hauled in the back of his station wagon. Some neighbors thought he was wasting his money. One told the local paper that Brandt was "planting shade for people who haven't been born yet."

Brandt seemed to take that as encouragement. He persuaded his students to join him on Saturday mornings, and over the next thirty years they put roughly four thousand trees into the ground. He kept a ledger of every one: the species, the address, the date, and the name of the student who planted it. When a tree died, he noted the likely cause and tried a hardier kind in its place.

The results are easy to see today. Elm Avenue, once the hottest street in town, now lies under a continuous green canopy, and city records show that summer temperatures on shaded blocks run several degrees cooler than on the few that remain open. Former students still stop at "their" trees to read the small metal tags Brandt fixed to the trunks.

Brandt never held public office and rarely spoke at meetings. His gift to Halvern arrived slowly, one sapling at a time, and it was the kind of work that only a very patient person could finish. It is fitting that the ledger now sits in a glass case at the town hall, open to the page where he wrote his first entry.

item.passage:
Every quarter at Fenwick Middle School, the principal reads the honor roll over the loudspeaker during morning announcements. It takes about six minutes. Students in every classroom sit and listen as some two hundred names are called in alphabetical order, from Abbott to Zuniga. I think the school should stop doing this and post the list online and in the front hall instead.

My reason starts with what those six minutes actually feel like. When your own name is read, you get a quick flush of pride, and then you wait through nearly two hundred more. Meanwhile, the students who missed the list are sitting in the same rooms, waiting for the reading to end. Teachers have told me that the rest of that morning is one of the hardest stretches of the quarter to teach.

Some people argue that public recognition is exactly what pushes students to work harder, and that ending the reading would send the message that grades matter less. I take that argument seriously. Recognition does matter, and the students on the list earned it. But a loudspeaker is a strange way to deliver it. Hearing your name as one of two hundred, in a room where half your classmates are staring at their desks, is hardly the same as being congratulated. A posted list lets families find their child's name, take a photo, and celebrate at home, where the praise can actually sink in.

There is also the matter of time. Six minutes, four times a year, adds up to almost half an hour of class time that could go to the morning work the reading interrupts. That is a modest number, but it comes from the part of the day when students are most alert.

Fenwick already posts sports results and club news on the school website, and nobody complains that the soccer team goes unrecognized. The honor roll deserves the same respect: a permanent page that students can return to, rather than a list read aloud and gone in six minutes. Let's celebrate the students who earned it without making the morning harder for everyone else.
